She said to the servant, ‘Who is that man coming through the field to meet us?’ The servant said, ‘He is my master.’ Then she took a veil and covered herself.
The servant told Isaac everything he had done.
Isaac entered the house of Sarah his mother and took Rebekah, and she became his wife. He loved her, and Isaac was comforted over Sarah his mother.
Abraham took another wife, whose name was Keturah.
She bore him Zimran, Jokshan, Medan, Midian, Ishbak, and Shuah.
Jokshan fathered Sheba, Teman, and Dedan. The sons of Dedan were Raguel, Nabdeel, Asshurim, Letushim, and Leummim.
The sons of Midian were Ephah, Epher, Hanoch, Abida, and Eldaah. All these were sons of Keturah.
Abraham gave all his possessions to his son Isaac.
Abraham gave gifts to the sons of his concubines, and while he was still alive, he sent them away from his son Isaac, eastward to the land of the east.
These are the years of Abraham’s life that he lived: one hundred and seventy-five years.
Abraham breathed his last and died at a good old age, old and full of days, and was gathered to his people.
His sons Isaac and Ishmael buried him in the double cave in the field of Ephron son of Zohar the Hittite, opposite Mamre.
The field and the cave were those that Abraham acquired from the sons of Heth. There they buried Abraham and Sarah his wife.
After Abraham’s death, God blessed his son Isaac, and Isaac lived by the Well of the Vision.
These are the descendants of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, whom Hagar the Egyptian, Sarah’s maidservant, bore to Abraham.
These are the names of Ishmael’s sons, by the names of their clans: Ishmael’s firstborn, Nebaioth, then Kedar, Adbeel, and Mibsam,
Mishma, Dumah, and Massa,
Hadad, Tema, Jetur, Naphish, and Kedemah.
These are Ishmael’s sons, and these are their names according to their settlements and their tents: twelve chiefs according to their clans.
The years of Ishmael’s life were one hundred and thirty-seven years. He breathed his last and died, and was gathered to his people.
He lived from Havilah to Shur, which is opposite Egypt, as one goes toward Assyria. He lived opposite all his brothers.
These are the descendants of Isaac son of Abraham. Abraham fathered Isaac.
Isaac was forty years old when he took Rebekah as his wife, the daughter of Bethuel the Syrian from Mesopotamia of the Syrians, and the sister of Laban the Syrian.
Isaac pleaded with the Lord for his wife Rebekah, because she was barren. God heard him, and his wife Rebekah conceived.
The children were moving about inside her, and she said, “If it is to be this way for me, why is this happening to me?” She went to inquire of the Lord.
The Lord said to her, “Two nations are in your womb, and two peoples will be separated from your body. One people will prevail over the other, and the older will serve the younger.”
When her days for giving birth were fulfilled, there were two sons in her womb.
The firstborn son came out reddish, covered all over like a shaggy hide, and she named him Esau. Then his brother came out, his hand holding Esau’s heel, and she named him Jacob.
Isaac was sixty years old when Rebekah gave birth to them.
The children grew up. Esau was a man skilled in hunting, a man of the wild, while Jacob was an unassuming man who stayed at home.
Isaac loved Esau because his game was food for him, but Rebekah loved Jacob.
Jacob had cooked a stew, and Esau came in from the field exhausted.
Esau said to Jacob, “Let me taste some of that red stew, because I am exhausted.” That is why he was named Edom.
Jacob said to Esau, “Sell me your birthright today.”
Esau said, “Look, I am about to die. What use will that birthright be to me?”
Jacob said to him, “Swear to me today.” He swore to him, and Esau sold his birthright to Jacob.
Jacob gave Esau bread and lentil broth. He ate and drank, got up, and went away. Thus Esau despised his birthright.
There was a famine in the land, apart from the earlier famine that occurred in Abraham’s time. Isaac went to Abimelech, king of the Philistines, in Gerar.
The Lord appeared to him and said, “Do not go down to Egypt. Instead, live in the land that I will tell you.
Stay as a foreigner in this land, and I will be with you and bless you, for I will give all these lands to you and your descendants. I will fulfill the oath that I swore to Abraham your father.
I will multiply your descendants like the stars of heaven and give all these lands to your descendants. Through your descendants all the nations of the earth will be blessed,
because Abraham your father obeyed my voice and kept my commands, my commandments, my statutes, and my laws.”
Isaac lived among the people of Gerar.

The men of the place asked about Rebekah his wife, and he said, “She is my sister.” He was afraid to say, “She is my wife,” lest the men of the place kill him because of Rebekah, for she was beautiful.
He remained there a long time. Abimelech, king of the Philistines, looked out through a window and saw Isaac playing with Rebekah his wife.
Abimelech called Isaac and said to him, “So she was your wife! Why did you say, ‘She is my sister’?” Isaac said to him, “Because I thought I might die because of her.”
Abimelech said to him, “Why have you done this to us? One of my people almost slept with your wife, and you would have brought unintentional guilt upon us.”
Abimelech commanded all his people, saying, “Anyone who touches this man or his wife shall be put to death.”
Isaac sowed seed in that land and reaped a hundredfold yield of barley that year. The Lord blessed him.
The man prospered and continued to advance and grow until he became very great.
He had flocks of sheep, herds of cattle, and abundant crops, and the Philistines envied him.
The Philistines stopped up all the wells that his servants had dug in the days of Abraham his father and filled them with earth.
Abimelech said to Isaac, “Go away from us, for you have become much stronger than we are.”
Isaac left that place and settled in the valley of Gerar, where he lived.

Isaac again dug the wells of water that the servants of his father Abraham had dug and that the Philistines had stopped up after the death of his father Abraham. He gave them the same names that Abraham his father had given them.
Isaac’s servants dug in the valley of Gerar and found a well of flowing water there.
The shepherds of Gerar quarreled with Isaac’s shepherds, saying that the well was theirs. He named the well “Deprivation,” because they were depriving him of it.
He moved away from there and dug another well of water. They disputed over that one too, and he named it “Hostility.”
He moved away from there and dug another well, and they did not quarrel over it. He named it “Peace,” saying, “Now the Lord has made room for us and caused us to increase in the land.”
He went up from there to the Well of the Oath.
The Lord appeared to him that night and said, “I am the God of your father. Do not be afraid, for I am with you. I will bless you and multiply your descendants for the sake of Abraham your father.”
He built an altar there and called on the name of the Lord. He pitched his tent there, and Isaac’s servants dug a well there.
Abimelech came to him from Gerar, with Ahuzzath, his palace steward, and Phicol, the commander of his army.
Isaac said to them, “Why have you come to me, since you hated me and drove me away from you?”
They said, “We have clearly seen that the Lord was with you, and we said, ‘Let there be an oath between us, between us and you, and let us make a covenant with you
that you will do us no harm, just as we did you no wrong, but treated you well and sent you away in peace. And now you are blessed by the Lord.’”
He made a feast for them, and they ate and drank.
They rose early the next morning and swore an oath to one another. Isaac sent them away, and they departed from him in peace.
That same day Isaac’s servants came and told him about the well they had dug, saying, “We have found water.”
He named it Oath. That is why the name of that city is Well of the Oath to this day.
Esau was forty years old, and he took as wives Judith, the daughter of Beeri the Hittite, and Basemath, the daughter of Elon the Hivite.
They made life bitter for Isaac and Rebekah.
When Isaac grew old and his eyes became too weak to see, he called Esau, his older son, and said to him, “My son.” He answered, “Here I am.”
He said to him, “Look, I have grown old, and I do not know the day of my death.
Now take your equipment, your bow and quivers, and go out into the countryside and hunt game for me.
Prepare tasty food for me, just as I like it, and bring it to me so that I may eat and my soul may bless you before I die.”
Rebekah heard Isaac speaking with his son. Esau went out into the countryside to hunt game for his father.
Rebekah spoke to Jacob, her son, and said, “Look, I heard your father speaking with your brother and saying,
‘Bring me game and prepare tasty food for me, so that I may eat and bless you before the Lord before I die.’
Now, my son, listen to me and do as I command you.
Go to the flock and bring me two tender, choice young goats from there, and I will prepare them as tasty food for your father, just as he likes it.
You will bring it to your father, and he will eat, so that your father may bless you before he dies.”
Jacob said to Rebekah, his mother, “My brother Esau is a hairy man, and I am smooth-skinned.
Perhaps my father will feel me, and I will seem to him like a mocker, and I will bring a curse upon myself rather than a blessing.”
His mother said to him, “Let that curse fall on me, my son. Only listen to my voice, and go and bring them to me.”
He went and brought them to his mother, and she prepared savory food just as his father liked.
Rebekah took the fine robe of her older son, which she had with her in the house, and dressed Jacob, her younger son, in it.
And she put the young goats’ skins on his arms and on his bare neck.
And she put the savory food and the bread she had made into the hands of her son Jacob.
And he brought them to his father and said, “My father.” He said, “Here I am.” And he said, “Who are you, my son?”
Jacob said to his father, “I am Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you told me. Get up, sit, and eat some of my game, so that your soul may bless me.”
And Isaac said to his son, “How did you find it so quickly, my son?” He said, “Because the Lord God provided it before me.”
And Isaac said to Jacob, “Come near, so that I may feel you, my son, to see whether you are my son Esau or not.”
Jacob approached his father Isaac, and he felt him and said, “The voice is Jacob’s voice, but the hands are Esau’s hands.”
He did not recognize him, because his hands were hairy like the hands of his brother Esau, and he blessed him.
And he said, “Are you my son Esau?” He said, “I am.”
And he said, “Bring it to me, and I will eat some of your game, my son, so that my soul may bless you.” He brought it to him, and he ate. And he brought him wine, and he drank.
And his father Isaac said to him, “Come near and kiss me, my son.”
And he approached and kissed him. He smelled the scent of his clothes and blessed him, saying, “See, the scent of my son is like the scent of a bountiful field that the Lord has blessed.
And may God give you of the dew of heaven and of the richness of the earth, and an abundance of grain and wine.

And may nations serve you, and rulers bow down to you. Be lord over your brother, and may your father’s sons bow down to you. Whoever curses you, let him be cursed, and whoever blesses you, let him be blessed.”
And after Isaac had finished blessing his son Jacob, just as Jacob left the presence of his father Isaac, his brother Esau came back from hunting.
He too prepared savory food and brought it to his father. He said to his father, “Let my father rise and eat some of his son’s game, so that your soul may bless me.”
And his father Isaac said to him, “Who are you?” He said, “I am your firstborn son, Esau.”
And Isaac was utterly astonished and said, “Then who was it who hunted game for me and brought it to me? I ate some of everything before you came, and I blessed him, and he shall be blessed.”
And when Esau heard the words of his father Isaac, he cried out loudly and very bitterly and said to his father, “Bless me too, father!”
He said, “Your brother came deceitfully and took your blessing.”

And he said, “He was rightly named Jacob, for he has deceived me these two times: he took my birthright, and now he has taken my blessing.” And Esau said to his father, “Have you not left any blessing for me, father?”
Isaac answered and said to Esau, “Since I have made him your lord and made all his brothers his servants, and have sustained him with grain and wine, what shall I do for you, my son?”
Esau said to his father, “Do you have only one blessing, father? Bless me too, father!” And as Isaac was deeply moved, Esau raised his voice and wept.
His father Isaac answered and said to him, “See, your dwelling shall be of the richness of the earth and of the dew of heaven above.
And you shall live by your sword and serve your brother. But when you break free, you shall loosen his yoke from your neck.”

And Esau held a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing with which his father had blessed him. And Esau said in his heart, “Let the days of mourning for my father draw near, so that I may kill my brother Jacob.”
The words of her older son Esau were reported to Rebekah, and she sent for her younger son Jacob and said to him, “Look, your brother Esau is threatening to kill you.
Now, my son, listen to my voice. Rise and go to Mesopotamia, to my brother Laban in Haran.”
And stay with him for many days, until your brother’s furious anger against you subsides.
And he forgets what you did to him. Then I will send for you and bring you back from there, lest I be bereaved of both of you in one day.

And Rebekah said to Isaac, “I am weary of my life because of the daughters of the descendants of Heth. If Jacob takes a wife from those daughters of Heth, from the daughters of this land, what reason will I have to live?”
Isaac called Jacob to him, blessed him, and commanded him, saying, “Do not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites here.
Instead, get up and go to Syrian Mesopotamia, to the house of Bethuel, your mother’s father, and take a wife for yourself from there, from the daughters of Laban, your mother’s brother.
And may my God bless you, make you fruitful, and multiply you, so that you become an assembly of nations.
And may he give you the blessing of Abraham my father, to you and to your offspring after you, so that you may inherit the land where you live as a foreigner, which God gave to Abraham.”
And Isaac sent Jacob away, and he went to Syrian Mesopotamia, to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Syrian and the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau.

And Esau saw that Isaac had blessed Jacob and that Jacob had gone to Syrian Mesopotamia to take a wife for himself from there, and that, when blessing him, Isaac had commanded him, saying, “Do not take a wife from the daughters of the Canaanites here.”
And Jacob obeyed his father and his mother and went to Syrian Mesopotamia.
And Esau saw that the daughters of the Canaanites were displeasing to Isaac his father.
Esau went to Ishmael and took Mahalath, the daughter of Ishmael, Abraham’s son, and the sister of Nebaioth, as his wife, in addition to his other wives.
Jacob left Beersheba and went to Haran.
And he came to a certain place and slept there, because the sun was setting. He took some of the stones of that place, put them at his head, and slept in that place.
And he saw a vision: there was a ladder set on the earth, whose top reached heaven, and the angels of God were ascending and descending on it.

And the Lord stood upon it and said, “I am the Lord, the God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. Do not be afraid, for I will give the land on which you are sleeping to you and to your offspring.
And your offspring will be like the sand of the earth and will spread out to the west, east, north, and south. And all the nations of the earth will be blessed through you and through your offspring.
And behold, I am with you, to guard you on all your journeys, wherever you go, and I will bring you back to this land. For I will not leave you until I have done everything I have told you.”
And Jacob awoke from his sleep and said, “The Lord is in this place, and I did not know it.”
He was struck with fear and said, “How awesome this place is! This is nothing other than the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.”
And Jacob rose in the morning, took the stone that he had placed at his head, set it up as a pillar, and poured oil on its top.
And Jacob called that place “House of God.” Previously, the name of that city was Luz.
And Jacob made a vow, saying, “If the Lord God is with me and keeps me safe on this journey that I am taking, and gives me bread to eat and clothing to wear,
“and brings me back safely to my father’s house, then the Lord will be my God.”
Then this stone, which I have set up as a pillar, will be a house of God for me, and of everything you give me I will give you a tenth.”
And Jacob lifted his feet and went to the land of the east, to Laban, the son of Bethuel the Syrian and the brother of Rebekah, the mother of Jacob and Esau.
And he looked, and there was a well in the field, with three flocks of sheep lying beside it. They watered the sheep from that well, and a large stone lay over the mouth of the well.
All the flocks would gather there, and they would roll the stone away from the mouth of the well and water the sheep. Then they would put the stone back in its place over the mouth of the well.
Jacob said to them, “Brothers, where are you from?” They said, “We are from Haran.”
He said to them, “Do you know Laban, the son of Nahor?” They said, “We know him.”
He said to them, “Is he well?” They said, “He is well. Look, his daughter Rachel is coming with the sheep.”
Jacob said, “There is still much of the day left; it is not yet time to gather the sheep. Water the sheep and go pasture them.”
They said, “We cannot until all the shepherds gather and roll the stone away from the mouth of the well. Then we will water the sheep.”
While he was speaking with them, Rachel, Laban’s daughter, came with her father’s sheep, for she tended her father’s sheep.

When Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of Laban, his mother’s brother, and the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother, Jacob approached, rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well, and watered the sheep of Laban, his mother’s brother.
Jacob kissed Rachel, raised his voice, and wept.
Jacob told Rachel that he was her father’s brother and Rebekah’s son. She ran and told her father these things.
When Laban heard the name of Jacob, his sister’s son, he ran to meet him, embraced him, kissed him, and brought him into his house. Jacob told Laban all these things.
Laban said to him, “You are of my bones and of my flesh.” And he stayed with him for a month.
Laban said to Jacob, “Because you are my brother, you should not work for me for nothing. Tell me what your wages should be.”
Laban had two daughters. The older was named Leah, and the younger was named Rachel.
Leah’s eyes were watery, but Rachel had a fine figure and a beautiful face.
Jacob loved Rachel and said, “I will serve you seven years for Rachel, your younger daughter.”
Laban said to him, “It is better to give her to you than to give her to a stranger. Stay with me.”
Jacob served seven years for Rachel, and they seemed to him like only a few days because he loved her.
Jacob said to Laban, “Give me my wife, for my time is completed, so that I may go in to her.”
Laban gathered all the men of the place and held a wedding feast.
When evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and brought her to Jacob, and Jacob went in to her.
Laban gave his servant Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her maid.
When morning came, there was Leah! Jacob said to Laban, “What have you done? Did I not serve you for Rachel? Why did you deceive me?”
Laban said, “It is not the custom in our land to give the younger before the older.”
Now complete another seven years with her, and I will give you the other one too, in return for the work you will do for me for another seven years.”
Jacob did so and completed another seven years with her, and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
Laban gave his servant Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maid.
And he slept with Rachel and loved Rachel more than Leah, and he served him for another seven years.
When the Lord saw that Leah was hated, he opened her womb, but Rachel was barren.
Leah conceived and bore Jacob a son, and she named him Reuben, saying, "Because the Lord has seen my suffering, my husband will now love me."
Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a second son, and she said, "Because the Lord heard that I was hated, he has also given me this son." And she named him Simeon.
And she conceived and bore a son, and she said, "Now my husband will be with me, because I have borne him three sons." For this reason she named him Levi.
And she conceived again and bore a son, and she said, "This time I will give thanks to the Lord." And she named him Judah, and she stopped bearing children.
When Rachel saw that she had borne Jacob no children, she became jealous of her sister and said to Jacob, “Give me children, or I will die.”
Jacob became angry with Rachel and said to her, "Am I in God's place, who has withheld the fruit of your womb?"
Rachel said to Jacob, "Here is my maidservant Bilhah. Sleep with her, and she will give birth on my knees, so that I too may have children through her."
And she gave him her maidservant Bilhah as a wife, and Jacob slept with her.
Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, conceived and bore Jacob a son.
Rachel said, "God has vindicated me and heard my voice and given me a son." For this reason she named him Dan.
Bilhah, Rachel's maidservant, conceived again and bore Jacob a second son.
Rachel said, “God has helped me, for I wrestled with my sister and prevailed.” And she named him Naphtali.
When Leah saw that she had stopped bearing children, she took her maidservant Zilpah and gave her to Jacob as a wife.
Zilpah, Leah's maidservant, conceived and bore Jacob a son.
Leah said, "My good fortune is with me!" And she named him Gad.
Zilpah, Leah's maidservant, conceived and bore Jacob another son, his second by her.
Leah said, "I am blessed, for women will call me blessed." And she named him Asher—greatness.
Reuben went out during the wheat harvest and found mandrake fruit in the field, and he brought it to Leah his mother. Rachel said to Leah her sister, "Give me some of your son's mandrakes."

Leah said, "Is it not enough for you that you have taken my husband? Will you also take my son's mandrakes?" Rachel said, "Not so. He will sleep with you tonight in exchange for your son's mandrakes."

When Jacob came in from the field in the evening, Leah went out to meet him and said, "You must sleep with me today, because I have hired you in exchange for my son's mandrakes." And he slept with her that night.
God listened to Leah, and she conceived and bore Jacob a fifth son.
Leah said, "God has given me my wages because I gave my maidservant to my husband." And she named him Issachar, which means wages.
Leah conceived again and bore Jacob a sixth son.
Leah said, "God has given me a good gift. From now on my husband will love me, because I have borne him six sons." And she named him Zebulun.
After that she bore a daughter and named her Dinah.
And God remembered Rachel, and God listened to her and opened her womb.
And she conceived and bore Jacob a son. Rachel said, “God has taken away my disgrace.”
And she named him Joseph, saying, “May God add another son for me.”
And when Rachel had given birth to Joseph, Jacob said to Laban, “Let me go, so that I may return to my own place and my own country.
Give me my wives and my children, for whom I served you, so that I may leave, for you yourself know the service I have rendered you.”
Laban said to him, “If I have found favor in your eyes—I have learned by divination that God has blessed me because of your presence.”
Laban said, “Tell me what wages you want from me, and I will pay them.”
Jacob said to him, “You know how much I have served you and how your livestock have fared under my care.
For you had little before I came, but it has increased greatly, and the Lord God has blessed you because of my presence. Now, when shall I provide a household for myself?”
Laban said to him, “What shall I give you?” Jacob said to him, “Give me nothing. Only do this one thing for me, and I will again pasture your livestock and keep them.

Let all your livestock pass before you today, and separate out every speckled and gray sheep, and every solid-colored grazing animal among the lambs. All the speckled ones among the lambs and the spotted ones among the goats shall be my wages.
My honesty will be evident tomorrow, when my wages are before you: every goat that is not speckled or spotted, and every lamb that is not gray-speckled, shall be counted as stolen if found with me.”
Laban said to him, “Let it be according to your word.”

And that day he separated out the gray and spotted male goats, all the gray and spotted female goats, all the white ones among them, and all the solid-colored lambs, and gave them into the hands of his sons.
And he put a three-day journey between them and Jacob, while Jacob pastured Laban’s remaining livestock.

Jacob took fresh branches of storax, walnut, and plane trees. Jacob peeled them, and they became white. He scraped the green bark from the branches, and the white that he scraped from the colored surface showed on the branches.
And he placed the branches he had scraped in the water troughs, so that when the livestock came to drink water, they would mate facing the branches as they came to drink.
The flocks conceived before the rods, and the flocks bore young that were gray-speckled, spotted, and mottled.
Jacob separated the lambs and set them before the ewes, together with the gray ram and all the gray-speckled lambs. He kept his own flocks separate and did not mix them with Laban’s livestock.
And whenever the livestock mated and conceived, Jacob placed the branches before the livestock in the troughs, so that they would mate facing the branches.
But when the livestock gave birth, he did not put them there. The unmarked animals belonged to Laban, and the marked animals to Jacob.
And the man became exceedingly prosperous, and he had very many sheep and cattle, male and female servants, camels, and donkeys.
Jacob heard the words of Laban’s sons, who were saying, “Jacob has taken everything belonging to our father, and from our father’s possessions he has acquired all this wealth for himself.”
And Jacob saw Laban’s face, and it was no longer toward him as it had been before.
The Lord God said to Jacob, “Return to the land of your father and to your kindred, and I will be with you.”
Jacob sent for Rachel and Leah and called them to the field where the livestock were.
He said to them, “I see that your father’s face is not toward me as it was yesterday and the day before, but the God of my father has been with me.”
“And you yourselves know that I have served your father with all my strength.”
Your father opposed me and changed my wages for those ten spotted animals, but God did not allow him to harm me.
If he said, “The spotted ones shall be your wages,” all the flocks gave birth to spotted young. And if he said, “The white ones shall be your wages,” all the flocks gave birth to white young.
And God took away all your father’s flocks and gave them to me.
When the flocks were mating, I saw with my own eyes in a dream that the male goats and rams mounting the ewes and female goats were piebald, speckled, and gray-spotted.
And the angel of God said to me in the vision, “Jacob!” And I said, “What is it?”

And he said, “Look with your own eyes and see how the male goats and rams mounting the ewes and female goats are piebald, gray-spotted, and speckled, for I have seen everything Laban has been doing to you.
I am the God who appeared to you in the place of God, where you anointed the pillar for me and made vows. Now rise, leave this land, and go to the land of your birth, and I will be with you.”
Rachel and Leah answered him, saying, “Do we still have any share or inheritance in our father’s house?
Does he not regard us as strangers? For he sold us and devoured our money.”
“All the wealth and glory that God has taken from our father shall belong to us and our children. Now do whatever God has told you.”
Jacob rose, took his wives and children, and put them on camels.
And he set out with all his belongings and all the property he had acquired in Syrian Mesopotamia, to go to his father Isaac in the land of the Canaanites.
Laban had gone to shear his flocks, and Rachel stole her father’s idols.
And Jacob deceived Laban, his father-in-law, by not telling him that he was leaving.
He departed with everything he had, crossed the River, and headed toward the mountain of Gilead.
On the third day, Laban the Syrian was told that Jacob had departed.
Taking his brothers with him, he pursued Jacob for a seven-day journey and caught up with him on the mountain of Gilead.
God came to Laban the Syrian in a vision at night and said to him, “Take care not to speak abusively to Jacob.”
Laban caught up with Jacob. Jacob had pitched his tent on the mountain, and Laban encamped with his brothers on the mountain of Gilead.
Laban said to Jacob, “Why have you done this? Why did you leave me secretly, deceive me, and drive away my daughters like captives taken by the sword?
If you had told me, I would have sent you off with joy and with tambourine and lyre players.
Was I not even worthy to kiss my sons and daughters? You have acted foolishly.
Now I have the power to harm you, but yesterday the God of your father spoke to me, saying, ‘Take care not to speak abusively to Jacob.’
Now you have gone away because you longed so greatly to return to your father’s house. But why did you steal my gods?”
Jacob answered Laban, saying, “Because I was afraid. I thought you might take your daughters away from me, along with everything I have.”

And Jacob said, “Whoever you find your gods with shall not live before our brothers. Now identify any of your belongings that are with me, and take them.” But Laban recognized nothing of his with him. Jacob did not know that Rachel, his wife, had stolen them.
Laban went in and searched Jacob’s tent, Leah’s tent, and the tents of the two concubines, but found nothing. He left Leah’s tent and entered Rachel’s tent.
Rachel had taken the idols, put them under the camel’s saddlecloth, and sat on them. Laban searched the whole tent but found nothing.
She said to her father, “Do not be offended, my lord, that I cannot rise to my feet before you, for I am having my monthly period.” Laban searched the whole tent but did not find the idols.
Jacob became angry and argued with Laban. Jacob answered and said to Laban, “What is my offense, or what are my sins, that you have pursued me so relentlessly?
You have searched all my possessions. What have you found in my tent that belongs to you? Put it here before my relatives and your relatives, and let them judge between the two of us.
For these twenty years I have been with you. Your sheep and goats did not become barren, and I did not eat the rams of your flock.
I did not bring you animals torn by wild beasts; instead, I bore the loss myself, both for what was stolen by day and for what was stolen by night.
By day I suffered from the scorching heat, and by night from the cold, and sleep fled from my eyes.
For these twenty years I have been in your household. I worked fourteen years for your daughters and six years for your flocks, and you cheated me over my wages ten times.

If the God of my father, the God of Abraham and the Fear of Isaac, had not been with me, you would surely have sent me away empty-handed now. But God saw my suffering and the labor of my hands, and he rebuked you yesterday.”

Laban answered and said to Jacob, “These daughters are my daughters, these sons are my sons, and these flocks are my flocks. Everything you see belongs to me and to these daughters of mine. Now what can I do today to them or to their children, whom I fathered?
But now come, let us make a covenant, you and I, and let it be a witness between me and you.” And he said to him, “Look, there is no one here between us, but God is a witness between me and you.”
Jacob took a stone and set it up as a pillar.
He said to his relatives, “Gather stones.” They gathered stones and made a mound, and they ate and drank there on the mound.
Laban called it “Heap of Testimony,” and Jacob called it “Witness Heap.”

Laban said to him, “This mound is a witness between me and you today.” Laban called it “Mound of Testimony,” and Jacob called it “Witness Mound.” Laban said to Jacob, “Look, this mound and this pillar that I have set up between me and you: this mound is a witness, and this pillar is a witness.” Therefore the mound was named “Testimony,”
and “The Watch,” of which he said, “May God watch between me and you, for we are parting from one another.
If you mistreat my daughters, or if you take wives besides my daughters, beware: there is no one with us who sees. Let God be a witness between me and you.”
Laban said to Jacob, “Look at this heap and this pillar that we have set up between me and you.
Let this heap be a witness, and this pillar a witness, that I will not pass beyond this heap, and that you must not pass beyond this mound and this pillar with evil intent.
May the God of Abraham and the God of Nahor, the God of their fathers, judge between us.” Jacob swore by the Fear of his father Isaac.
Jacob offered a sacrifice on the mountain and called his brothers to eat bread. They ate and drank and spent the night there on the mountain.
Laban rose early the next morning, kissed his sons and daughters, and blessed them. Then Laban departed and returned to his own place.
Jacob went on his way. He looked and saw God’s army encamped, and the angels of God came to meet him.
When Jacob saw them, he said, “This is God’s camp.” And he named that place “Camps.”
Jacob sent messengers ahead of him to his brother Esau, to the land of Seir, in the territory of Edom.
He instructed them, saying, “Say this to my lord Esau: ‘Your servant Jacob says this: I have stayed with Laban and remained there until now.
I have cattle, sheep, donkeys, male servants, and female servants. I have sent word to my lord Esau so that your servant may find favor with you.’”
The messengers returned to Jacob and said, “We went to your brother Esau, and he is coming to meet you with four hundred men.”
Jacob was frightened and distressed. He divided the people who were with him, along with the cattle, sheep, and camels, into two camps.
Jacob said, “If Esau comes to the first camp and attacks it, the second camp will escape.”
Jacob said, “God of my father Abraham and God of my father Isaac, Lord, you who said to me, ‘Go to the land of your birth, and I will do you good,’
I am not worthy of all the righteousness and faithfulness you have shown your servant. For I crossed this Jordan with only a staff in my hand, and now, look, I have become two camps.
Deliver me from the hand of my brother Esau, for I am afraid of him, lest he come and strike me down, mother and child alike.
You said, ‘I will do you good and make your descendants like the sand of the sea, which is too plentiful to count.’”
He slept there that night. From what he had brought with his own hands, he took gifts and sent them to his brother Esau:
two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, two hundred ewes and twenty rams,
thirty camels that had given birth, together with their young, forty cows and ten bulls, twenty donkeys and ten foals.
He entrusted them to his servants, each herd separately, and said to his servants, “Go ahead of me, and keep the herds well apart from one another.”
He instructed the first servant, saying, “If my brother Esau meets you and asks, ‘Whose servant are you? Where are you going? And whose animals are these going ahead of you?’
say, ‘They are gifts from your servant Jacob, which he has sent to his lord Esau. He himself is coming behind us.’”
He instructed the first, the second, the third, and all those who were going ahead with the flocks, saying, “Speak these words to Esau when you meet him.

Also say, ‘Look, your servant Jacob is coming behind us.’” For he said, “I will appease him with these gifts going ahead of me, and afterward I will see his face. Perhaps he will treat me with honor.”
The gifts went on ahead of him, and he himself slept that night there in the camp.
He rose that same night, took his two wives, his two female servants, and his eleven sons, and crossed the ford of the Jabbok.
He took them across the ravine, along with everything he owned.
Jacob remained alone, and a man wrestled with him until morning.
When the man saw that he could not overcome him, he grasped the sinew of Jacob’s thigh and numbed it as he wrestled with him.
He said to him, “Let me go, for dawn has come.” Jacob said, “I will not let you go unless you bless me.”
He said to Jacob, “What is your name?” He answered, “Jacob.”
He said to him, “From now on they will no longer call you Jacob, but your name will be Israel, because you have held firm with God, and you will be strong against men.”
Jacob asked, saying, “Tell me your name.” He said, “Why do you ask about my name?” And he blessed him there.
Jacob called that place Vision of God, for he said, “I have seen God face to face, and my life has been spared.”
The sun rose upon him as he passed Vision of God, and he walked with a limp because of his hip.
For this reason, to this day the children of Israel do not eat the sinew that he numbed, which is over the hip socket, because he seized Jacob’s hip socket and numbed his sinew.
Jacob looked up and saw that his brother Esau was coming, with four hundred men. Jacob divided the children among Leah, Rachel, and the two maidservants.
He put the two maidservants and their sons in front, Leah and her sons behind them, and Rachel and Joseph last.
He himself went ahead of them and bowed to the ground seven times as he approached his brother.
Esau ran to meet him, embraced him and kissed him, fell upon his neck and kissed him, and they both wept.
He looked up, saw the women and children, and said, “What are these people to you?” Jacob said, “They are my children, with whom God has graciously blessed your servant.”
The maidservants and their sons approached and bowed down to him.
Leah and her sons approached and bowed down to him. Afterward Joseph and Rachel approached and bowed down to him.
He said, “What was that whole company I encountered?” Jacob said, “It was so that your servant might find favor with you.”
Esau said, “I too have plenty, brother. Keep what is yours.”
Jacob said, “No, please! If I have found favor with you, accept the gifts from my hands, for I have seen your face as one might see the face of God. Be pleased with me.
Accept my blessing that I have brought you, because God has been merciful to me, and I have everything.” He urged him, and he accepted it.
He said, “Let us set out and go, and let us take the straight road.”
Jacob said to him, “My lord himself knows that the children are young, and that the sheep and cattle have newborn young. If I drive them hard for even one day, all the flocks will die.
Let my lord go ahead of his servant. I will travel as I am able, as the road ahead allows, and as my children regain their strength, until I come to my lord in Seir.”
Esau said, “Then let me leave with you some of the people who are here with me.” Jacob said, “Why would I need that? It is enough that I have found favor with you, my lord.”
That day Esau returned on his way to Seir.
Jacob traveled to Booths and built houses for himself there, and shelters for his flocks. For this reason he called that place Booths.
Jacob came to Salem, a city of the Shechemites in the land of the Canaanites, when he returned from Mesopotamia of the Syrians, and settled opposite the city.
He bought the portion of the field where he pitched his tent from Hamor, the father of Shechem, for a hundred sheep.
He built an altar there and called upon the God of Israel.
Dinah, Leah’s daughter whom she had borne to Jacob, went out to observe the daughters of the land.
Shechem, the son of Hamor the Horite, who was the ruler of the land, saw her, took her, lay with her, and violated her.
He set his heart on Dinah, Jacob’s daughter, loved the young woman, and spoke to her in a way that pleased her.
Shechem spoke to his father Hamor and said, “Get this girl for me as a wife.”
Jacob heard that Hamor’s son had defiled his daughter Dinah. His sons were with the livestock in the field, and Jacob remained silent until they came.
Hamor, Shechem’s father, went out to Jacob to speak with him.

Jacob’s sons came from the field. When they heard, the men were distressed and deeply grieved, because he had committed a disgraceful act in Israel by sleeping with Jacob’s daughter. Such a thing must not be done.
Hamor spoke to them and said, “My son Shechem loves your daughter with all his soul. Now give her to him as a wife.
Intermarry with us: give us your daughters, and take our daughters for your sons.
Live among us. Look, the land is wide open before you. Settle here, trade in it, and acquire property in it.”
Shechem said to her father and her brothers, “May I find favor with you, and whatever you ask, we will give.
Make the bride-price and the gifts as large as you like, and I will give as much as you ask. Give me that girl as a wife.”
Jacob’s sons answered Shechem and his father Hamor deceitfully, speaking to them this way because they had defiled their sister Dinah.
Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, the sons of Leah, said, “We cannot do this thing, giving our sister to an uncircumcised man, because that would be a disgrace to us.
Only on this condition will we agree with you and live among you: you must become like us by circumcising every male among you.
Then we will give you our daughters and take wives for ourselves from your daughters. We will live with you and become one people.
But if you will not listen to us and be circumcised, we will take our daughters and leave.”
Their words seemed pleasing to Hamor and to Shechem, Hamor’s son.
The young man did not delay in doing this, because he was deeply attached to Jacob’s daughter. He was more honored than anyone else in his father’s household.
Hamor and his son Shechem came to the gate of their city, spoke to the men of their city, and said,
“These men are at peace with us. Let them settle in the land and trade in it, for the land is wide open before them. Let us take their daughters as wives for ourselves and give them our daughters.
But only on this condition will the men agree to live with us and become one people: every male among us must be circumcised, just as they are circumcised.”
“Will not their possessions, their livestock, and their four-footed animals become ours? Only let us become like them in this, and they will live among us.”
Everyone who went out through the gate of their city listened to Hamor and his son Shechem. Every male, everyone who went out through the gate of his city, had the flesh of his foreskin circumcised.
On the third day, while they were still in pain, two of Jacob’s sons, Simeon and Levi, Dinah’s brothers, each took his sword, entered the city armed, and killed every male.
They killed Hamor and his son Shechem with the edge of the sword, took Dinah from Shechem’s house, and left.
Jacob’s sons came upon the wounded men and plundered the city in which they had defiled their sister Dinah.
They took their cattle, sheep, and donkeys, both those in the city and whatever was outside.
They took captive all their slaves and their wives, and plundered all their furnishings and possessions, everything in the city and everything in the houses.

Jacob said to Simeon and Levi, “You have made me hated and appear shameless to all the inhabitants of this land, among the Canaanites and the Perizzites. I am few in number. Now if they gather against me and attack me, I will be utterly destroyed, both I and my household.”
They said, “But how could they drag our sister around like a prostitute?”
God said to Jacob, “Get up, go up to Bethel, and live there. Make an altar there to God, who appeared to you when you fled from your brother Esau.”
Jacob said to his household and to everyone who was with him, “Remove from among you the foreign gods that you have with you. Purify yourselves and change your clothes.
Let us get up and go up to Bethel, and make an altar there to God, who heard me on the day of my distress, who was with me and kept me safe on the journey I made.”
They gave Jacob the foreign gods they had in their hands and the earrings in their ears. Jacob hid them beneath the terebinth at Shechem and made them disappear to this day.
Israel set out from Shechem, and the terror of God fell upon the surrounding cities, so they did not pursue the sons of Israel.
Jacob came to Luz, which is in the land of the Canaanites—that is, Bethel—he and all the people who were with him.
He built an altar there and named the place Bethel, because God had appeared to him there when he was fleeing from his brother Esau.
Deborah, Rebekah’s nurse, died and was buried below Bethel, under the oak. He named it the Oak of Mourning.
God appeared to Jacob while he was there in Luz, when he came from Syrian Mesopotamia, and God blessed him.
God said to him, “Your name is Jacob. You will no longer be called Jacob, but your name will be Israel.” And he named him Israel.
God said to him, “I am your all-sufficient God. Be fruitful and multiply. Nations and assemblies of nations will come from you, and kings will come from your loins.
The land that I gave to Abraham and Isaac I will give to you. It will be yours, and I will give this land to your descendants after you.”
God went up from him, from the place where he had spoken with him.
Jacob set up a pillar in the place where he had spoken with him, a stone pillar. He offered offerings on it and poured oil over it.
He named the place where God had spoken with him Bethel.
He set out from Bethel, and as he approached the region of Chabratha to enter Ephrathah, Rachel gave birth and had a difficult labor.
While she was suffering in labor, the midwife said to her, “Take courage, for this too is a son for you.”
As her life was departing, for she died, she named him Son of My Sorrows, but his father named him Benjamin.
Rachel died and was buried on the road to Ephrathah, which is Bethlehem.
Jacob set up a pillar over her grave. It is the pillar of Rachel’s grave to this day.
Israel set out and pitched his tent beyond the tower of Eder.
While Israel was living in that land, Reuben went and slept with Bilhah, his father’s concubine. Israel heard about it, and it seemed evil to him. Jacob had twelve sons.
The sons of Leah: Reuben, Jacob’s firstborn, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun.
The sons of Rachel: Joseph and Benjamin.
And the sons of Bilhah, Rachel’s maidservant, were Dan and Naphtali.
And the sons of Zilpah, Leah’s maidservant, were Gad and Asher. These are the sons of Jacob who were born to him in Mesopotamia of Syria.
And Jacob came to his father Isaac at Mamre, to the city of the plain, [?] Hebron, in the land of the Canaanites, where Abraham and Isaac had lived as foreigners.
And all the days that Isaac lived were one hundred and eighty years.
And Isaac breathed his last and died and was gathered to his people, old and full of days. And his sons Esau and Jacob buried him.
And these are the descendants of Esau, who is Edom.
And Esau took wives for himself from the daughters of the Canaanites: Adah, the daughter of Elon the Hittite, and Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah, the son of Zibeon the Hivite,
and Basemath, the daughter of Ishmael, the sister of Nebaioth.
And Adah bore Eliphaz to Esau, and Basemath bore Reuel.
And Oholibamah bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah. These are the sons of Esau who were born to him in the land of the Canaanites.

And Esau took his wives, his sons and daughters, all the people of his household, all his possessions and livestock, and everything he had acquired and made in the land of the Canaanites, and left the land of the Canaanites, away from his brother Jacob.
For their possessions were too great for them to live together, and the land where they lived as foreigners could not support them because of the abundance of their possessions.
And Esau settled in Mount Seir. Esau himself is Edom.
And these are the descendants of Esau, the father of the Edomites, in Mount Seir.
And these are the names of Esau’s sons: Eliphaz, the son of Adah, Esau’s wife, and Reuel, the son of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
And the sons of Eliphaz were Teman, Omar, Zepho, Gatam, and Kenaz.
And Timna was the concubine of Eliphaz, Esau’s son, and she bore Amalek to Eliphaz. These are the sons of Adah, Esau’s wife.
And these are the sons of Reuel: Nahath, Zerah, Shammah, and Mizzah. These are the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
And these are the sons of Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah, the son of Zibeon, Esau’s wife. She bore Jeush, Jalam, and Korah to Esau.
These are the chiefs among Esau’s sons. The sons of Eliphaz, Esau’s firstborn: Chief Teman, Chief Omar, Chief Zepho, Chief Kenaz,
Chief Korah, Chief Gatam, Chief Amalek. These are the chiefs of Eliphaz in the land of the Edomites. These are the sons of Adah.

These are the sons of Reuel, Esau’s son: chief Nahath, chief Zerah, chief Shammah, and chief Mizzah. These are the chiefs descended from Reuel in the land of Edom; these are the sons of Basemath, Esau’s wife.
And these are the sons of Oholibamah, Esau’s wife: Chief Jeush, Chief Jalam, Chief Korah. These are the chiefs of Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah, Esau’s wife.
These are the sons of Esau, and these are their chiefs, and these are the sons of Edom.
And these are the sons of Seir the Horite, who lived in the land: Lotan, Shobal, Zibeon, Anah,
Dishon, Ezer, and Rishon. These are the chiefs of the Horite, the son of Seir, in the land of Edom.
The sons of Lotan were Hori and Hemam, and Lotan’s sister was Timna.
These are the sons of Shobal: Golam, Manahath, Ebal, Shepho, and Onan.
These are the sons of Zibeon: Aiah and Onan. This is the Onan who found the spring in the wilderness while tending the donkeys of his father Zibeon.
These are the children of Anah: Dishon and Oholibamah, the daughter of Anah.
These are the sons of Dishon: Amadan, Eshban, Ithran, and Cheran.
These are the sons of Ezer: Bilhan, Zukan, Osnikan, and Ukam.
These are the sons of Dishan: Uz and Aran.
These are the chiefs of the Horites: chief Lotan, chief Shobal, chief Zibeon, chief Anah,
chief Dishon, chief Ezer, and chief Dishan. These are the chiefs of the Horites, according to their domains, in the land of Edom.
These are the kings who reigned in the land of the Edomites before a king had reigned in Israel.
Bela son of Zippor reigned in Edom, and the name of his city was Dinhabah.
Bela died, and Jobab son of Zerah, from Bozrah, reigned in his place.
Jobab died, and Husham, from the land of the Temanites, reigned in his place.
Husham died, and Hadad son of Bedad, who defeated Midian in the plain of the Moabites, reigned in his place. The name of his city was Gethaim.
Hadad died, and Samlah, from Masrekah, reigned in his place.
Samlah died, and Saul, from Rehoboth by the riverbank, reigned in his place.
Saul died, and Baal-hanan son of Achbor reigned in his place.
Baal-hanan son of Achbor died, and Hadad son of Barad reigned in his place. The name of his city was Phogou, and the name of his wife was Mehetabel, daughter of Matred, son of Mezahab.

These are the names of the sons of Esau and the chiefs of Esau, by their peoples, according to their places, in their lands and in their clans, according to their names: chief Timna, chief Lotan, chief Jetheth,
chief Oholibamasa, chief Elah, chief Pinon,
chief Kenaz, chief Teman, chief Mazar,
chief Magdiel, and chief Zaboin. These are the chiefs of the Edomites, according to their dwelling places in the land they possessed. This is Esau, the father of Edom.
Jacob lived in the land where his father had lived as a foreigner, in the land of the Canaanites.

These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph was seventeen years old when he tended the flocks with his brothers. He was the younger one among the sons of Bilhah and the sons of Zilpah, his father’s wives, and they brought a bad report about Joseph to Israel, their father.
But Israel loved Joseph more than all his sons, because he was the son of his old age, and he made him a patterned robe.
When his brothers saw that their father loved him more than all his sons, they hated him and could not speak peaceably to him.
Joseph had a dream and told it to his brothers, and they hated him even more.
And he said to them, “Listen to the dream I had.”
“It seemed that we were binding sheaves in a field, and my sheaf rose and stood upright, while your sheaves gathered around and bowed down to my sheaf.”
His brothers said to him, “Will you really reign over us, or will you really rule us?” And they hated him even more because of his dreams and his words.
He had yet another dream and told it to his father and his brothers. He said, “Look, I had another dream: the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were bowing down to me.”
His father rebuked him and said, “What is this dream you have had? Will I and your mother and your brothers really come and bow down to you?”
His brothers were jealous of him, but his father kept his words in mind.
His brothers went to graze their father’s flocks in Shechem.
Israel said to Joseph, “Are not your brothers grazing the flocks at Shechem? Come, I will send you to them.” He said to him, “Here I am.”
Israel said to him, “Go and see whether your brothers and the flocks are well, and bring me word.” He sent him from the valley of Hebron, and he came to Shechem.
A man found him wandering in the field. The man asked him, “What are you looking for?”
He said, “I am looking for my brothers. Tell me where they are grazing their flocks.”
The man said to him, “They have moved on from here, and I heard them say, ‘Let us go to Dothan.’” Joseph went after his brothers and found them in Dothan.
His brothers saw him from a distance, before he came near them, and plotted together to kill him.
They said to one another, “Here comes the dreamer.”
“Come, let us kill him and throw him into one of these pits. We will say, ‘A wild beast devoured him,’ and we will see what becomes of his dreams.”
When Reuben heard this, he rescued him from their hands and said, “Let us not kill him.”

Reuben said to them, “Let us not shed blood. Instead, throw him into a pit here in the wilderness, but do not lay a hand on him.” This was so that he could rescue him from their hands and bring him back to his father.
When Joseph came to his brothers, they stripped him of his embroidered robe.
They took him and threw him into the pit. The pit was empty, and there was no water in it.
They sat down to eat bread. Looking up, they saw a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead. Their camels were loaded with incense, storax, and resin, which they were taking down to Egypt.
Judah said to his brothers, “What profit is there if we kill our brother and conceal his blood?”
“Come, let us sell him to the Ishmaelites, and let us not stain our hands with him, for he is our brother and our own flesh.” And his brothers listened to him.
Midianite merchants passed by, and they pulled Joseph up out of the pit and sold Joseph to the Ishmaelites for twenty coins. And they brought Joseph down to Egypt.
Reuben returned to the pit and did not find Joseph there in the pit. He tore his clothes.
He returned to his brothers and said, “The boy is not there! And now, where am I to go?”
They took Joseph’s robe, slaughtered a young goat, and dipped the robe in its blood.
They sent the embroidered robe to be taken to their father and said, “We found this. See whether this robe is your son’s or not.”
He recognized it and said, “It is my son’s robe. A fierce beast has eaten him; a beast has carried Joseph off.”
He tore his clothes, put sackcloth around his waist, and mourned for his son for many days.

All his sons and all his daughters gathered and came to comfort him, but he refused to be comforted. He said, “I will go down to my son in the underworld with this grief.” And his father wept for him.
The Midianites sold Joseph in Egypt to Potiphar, Pharaoh’s eunuch and chief executioner.
At that time Judah went down away from his brothers and went to a certain Adullamite named Hirah.
There Judah saw the daughter of a Canaanite man named Shua. He took her as his wife and slept with her.
She conceived and bore a son, and named him Er.
She conceived again and bore a son, and named him Onan.
She again bore a son, and named him Shelah. She was in Chezib when she bore them.
Judah took a wife for Er, his firstborn; her name was Tamar.
Er, Judah’s firstborn, was evil in the Lord’s sight, and God killed him.
Judah said to Onan, “Sleep with your brother’s wife, marry her, and raise up offspring for your brother.”
Onan knew that the offspring would not be his. Whenever he went in to his brother’s wife, he spilled his seed on the ground so as not to give his brother offspring.
What he did was evil in God’s sight, and he killed him too.

Judah said to Tamar, his daughter-in-law, “Remain a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up.” For he said, “Otherwise he too might die like his brothers.” Tamar went and lived in her father’s house.
Many days passed, and Shua’s daughter, Judah’s wife, died. After Judah was comforted, he went up to Timnah to the shearing of his sheep, together with Hirah the Adullamite, his shepherd.
Tamar, his daughter-in-law, was told, “Your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.”

She took off her widow’s clothes, put on a veil, adorned herself, and sat at the gate of Enaim, on the road to Timnah. For she saw that Shelah had grown up, but Judah had not given her to him as his wife.
When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute, because she had covered her face, and he did not recognize her.
He turned aside from the road toward her and said, “Let me sleep with you.” For he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law. She said, “What will you give me if you sleep with me?”
He said, “I will have a young goat from my flock brought to you.” She said, “Will you give me a pledge until you have it brought?”
He said, “What pledge shall I give you?” She said, “Your ring, your necklace, and the staff in your hand.” He slept with her, and she conceived by him.
She got up and went away, took off her wrap, and put on her widow’s clothes.
Judah sent the young goat through his shepherd, the Adullamite, to recover the pledge from the woman, but he did not find her.
He asked the men of the place, “Where is the prostitute who was at Enaim beside this road?” They said, “There was no prostitute anywhere here.”
He returned to Judah and said, “I did not find her. The men of the place also said, ‘There is no prostitute here.’”
Judah said, “Let her keep those things, lest we become a laughingstock. I sent this young goat, but you did not find her.”
After three months, Judah was told, “Your daughter-in-law Tamar has prostituted herself, and now she is pregnant through her prostitution.” Judah said, “Bring her out, and let her be burned.”
As they were taking her away, she sent word to her father-in-law, saying, “I am pregnant by the man to whom these pledges belong.” And she said, “Recognize whose ring, necklace, and staff these are.”
Judah recognized them and said, “She is more righteous than I, because I did not give her to my son Shelah.” And he did not sleep with her again.
When she was giving birth, there were two sons in her womb.
At the time of her delivery, one put out his hand first. The midwife took it and tied a scarlet thread around his hand, saying, “This one will come out first.”
When he drew his hand back, his brother immediately came out. She said, “Why has a barrier been broken through because of you?” And she named him Perez.
Afterward his brother came out, with the scarlet thread tied around his hand, and she named him Zerah.
Joseph was brought down to Egypt, and Potiphar, an Egyptian man, Pharaoh’s eunuch and captain of the guard, bought him from the Ishmaelites who had brought him there.
The Lord was with Joseph, and he was a successful man. He lived in the house of his master in Egypt.
His master saw that the Lord was with him and that the Lord made everything he did succeed in his hands.
Joseph found favor with his master because he pleased him. His master put him in charge of his house and entrusted everything he owned to Joseph.

After he put him in charge of his house and everything he owned, the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s house because of Joseph. The Lord’s blessing was upon everything he owned, both in the house and in the field.
He left everything he owned in Joseph’s hands and knew nothing about anything in his house except the food he ate. Joseph was handsome in face and very beautiful in appearance.
After these things, his master’s wife set her eyes on Joseph and said to him, “Sleep with me.”
But he refused and said to his master’s wife, “Look, because of me, my master concerns himself with nothing in his house, and he has entrusted everything to me.
There is no one in this house greater than I, and he has withheld nothing from me except you, because you are his wife. How could I do this great evil and sin before God?”
Although she spoke to Joseph day after day, he would not listen to her and sleep with her or even be near her.
One such day, Joseph went into the house to do his work, and none of the household was inside.
She seized his clothes and said, “Sleep with me.” But he left his clothes in her hands, fled, and went outside.
When she saw that he had left his clothes in her hands and had fled outside,
she called the members of the household and said, “Look! He has brought us a Hebrew servant to make a mockery of us. He came to me and said, ‘Sleep with me,’ and I cried out in a loud voice.
When he heard that I cried out loudly, he left his clothes beside me, fled, and went outside.”
She kept the clothes beside her until his master came home.
She spoke to him in these words, saying, “The Hebrew slave whom you brought to us came in to me to make sport of me, and said to me, ‘Lie with me.’
“But when he heard that I raised my voice and cried out, he left his garment with me and fled outside.”
When his master heard the words his wife spoke to him, saying, “This is what your servant did to me,” he became furious.
Joseph’s master took him and put him in prison, in the place where the king’s prisoners were held in confinement.
The Lord was with Joseph and showed him mercy, and he gave him favor with the prison warden.
The prison warden entrusted the prison to Joseph, along with all the prisoners who were there. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it.

The prison warden concerned himself with nothing in the prison because of him, since everything was in Joseph’s hands. For the Lord was with him, and whatever he did, the Lord made it succeed in his hands.
After these things, the chief cupbearer of the king of Egypt and the steward offended their master, the king of Egypt.
And Pharaoh was angry with his two eunuchs, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker.
And he put them in custody with the chief executioner, in the prison where Joseph was.
The captain of the guard entrusted them to Joseph, and he attended to them. They remained in that prison for some time.
And both of them dreamed, each his own dream, on the same night—the chief cupbearer and the chief baker of the king of Egypt—while they were there in prison.
Joseph came to them in the morning and saw that they were troubled.
He asked Pharaoh’s eunuchs, who were with him there in prison at his master’s house, “Why are your faces sad today?”
And they said to him, “We have had dreams, and there is no one to interpret them.” And Joseph said to them, “Do not their interpretations belong to God? Tell them to me.”
And the chief cupbearer told Joseph his dream and said, “In my vision, it seemed to me that there was a vine before me.
And on the vine were three very green branches, and it had three ripe clusters, clusters of grapes.
And Pharaoh’s cup was in my hand. I took the grapes and squeezed them into Pharaoh’s cup, and I put the cup into Pharaoh’s hands.”
And Joseph said to him, “This is its interpretation: the three branches are three days.
In three more days Pharaoh will remember your office and restore you to your position as cupbearer. You will place Pharaoh’s cup in his hand, just as you did formerly when you were his cupbearer.
But remember me when things go well for you, and show me kindness. Mention me before Pharaoh, and bring me out of this prison.
For I was kidnapped from the land of the Hebrews, and here I did nothing, yet they put me in this dungeon.”
When the chief baker saw that he had interpreted correctly, he said to Joseph, “I too saw something in a dream, and it seemed to me that I had three baskets of fine flour on my head.
And in the top basket were all kinds of food that King Pharaoh ate, prepared by the bakers, and the birds were eating it from the basket on my head.”
Joseph answered and said to him, “This is its interpretation: the three baskets are three days.
After three days Pharaoh will remove your head from you and hang you on a tree, and the birds of the sky will eat your flesh off you.”
And on the third day, which was Pharaoh’s birthday, he held a feast for all his servants, and he remembered the office of the chief cupbearer and the office of the chief baker among his servants.
And he restored the chief cupbearer to his office, and he put the cup into Pharaoh’s hand.
But he hanged the chief baker on a tree, just as Joseph had interpreted.
And the chief cupbearer did not remember Joseph, but forgot him.
And after two full years, Pharaoh had a dream. It seemed that he was standing at the river’s edge.
And behold, seven cows seemed to come up out of the river, beautiful in appearance and well-fed in body, and they grazed among the reeds there.
And behold, seven other cows came up after them out of the river, ugly in appearance and thin in body, and they grazed beside the other cows at the river’s edge.
And the seven cows that were ugly in appearance and thin in body ate the seven cows that were beautiful in appearance and well-fed. Then Pharaoh awoke.
And he went back to sleep and had a second dream. And behold, seven heads of grain were growing in one cluster, full and beautiful.
And behold, seven other ears of grain, thin and scorched by the hot wind, sprang up after them.
And the seven thin ears scorched by the hot wind swallowed the seven choice, plump ears. Pharaoh awoke, and it was a dream.
When morning came, he was troubled, and he sent for all the dream interpreters of Egypt and all its wise men. Pharaoh told them his dreams, but no one could interpret Pharaoh’s dreams.
The chief cupbearer spoke before Pharaoh and said, “Today I recall my offenses.
Pharaoh was angry with his servants and put us in prison in the house of the captain of the guard—me and the chief baker.
We both had dreams on the same night, he and I, each having his own dream.
There was a young Hebrew boy there with us, a servant of the captain of the guard. We told him, and he interpreted our dreams for us, giving each man the interpretation of his own dream.
And just as he interpreted them for us, so it happened: I returned to my office, and he was hanged on a tree.”
Pharaoh sent for Joseph, and they brought him out of the prison. They cut his hair and changed his robe, and he came before Pharaoh.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “I had a dream, and there is no one who can interpret it. But I have heard it said about you that when you hear dreams, you interpret them.”
Joseph answered Pharaoh, saying, “Without God there can be no answer concerning Pharaoh’s deliverance.”
Pharaoh spoke to Joseph and said, “In my vision, it seemed that I was standing on the bank of the river.
And it seemed that seven cows, fine in body and beautiful in appearance, came up out of the river and grazed there in the marshland.
And behold, seven other cows came up out of the river after them, miserable, very ugly in appearance, and thin in body. I have never seen uglier cows than these in all the land of Egypt.
The seven thin and ugly heifers ate the first seven heifers, which were beautiful and choice.
They went into their bellies, but could not be seen, and their appearance was as ugly as before. I awoke and then fell asleep again.
Once again I saw in a dream what seemed to be seven ears of grain growing in a single cluster, full and beautiful.
And seven other ears, blighted, shriveled, and scorched by the hot wind, sprang up beside them.
The seven shriveled ears scorched by the hot wind swallowed the seven beautiful, plump ears. I told the dream interpreters, but no one could interpret it for me.”
Joseph said to Pharaoh, “Pharaoh’s dream is one. God has shown Pharaoh what he is going to do.
The seven beautiful cows are seven years, and the seven beautiful ears of grain are seven years. Pharaoh’s dream is one.
The seven ugly, thin cows that came up after them are seven years, and the seven thin ears scorched by the hot wind will be seven years of famine.
This is what I said to Pharaoh: God has shown Pharaoh what he is going to do.
Behold, seven years of great abundance will come throughout the land of Egypt.
After that, seven years of famine will come, and the abundance will be forgotten throughout the land of Egypt. The famine will exhaust the land.
The abundance will not be remembered because of the famine that will follow it, for it will be very severe.
As for Pharaoh’s dream being repeated twice, it is because the matter is firmly established by God, and God will act quickly to bring it about.”
Now look for a wise man who can advise Pharaoh, and appoint him over the land of Egypt.
Let Pharaoh act and appoint officials over the land, and let them take a fifth of the crops of the land of Egypt during the seven years of abundance.
Let them gather all the food of the seven good years that are coming, and let the grain be gathered under Pharaoh’s authority, and let food be stored in the cities.
Let the food be kept for the land for the seven years of famine that will come upon the land of Egypt, so that the land will not perish from famine.
The proposal seemed good to Pharaoh and to all his servants.
Pharaoh said to all his servants, “Can we find a man like this, who has the Spirit of God within him?”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Since God has shown you all this, there is no man wiser or more discerning than you.
You shall be over my household, and all my people shall obey your commands. Only in the throne shall I be above you.”
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Look, today I have appointed you over the land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh took his ring from his hand and put it on Joseph’s hand. He clothed him in a robe of fine linen and put a gold necklace around his neck.
He had him ride in his second chariot, and a herald proclaimed before him. He appointed him over the land of Egypt.
Pharaoh said to Joseph, “Look, I am Pharaoh. Without you, no one shall lift his hands or his feet throughout the whole land of Egypt.”
Pharaoh named Joseph Zaphenath-paneah and gave him Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis, as his wife. Joseph went out from Pharaoh’s presence.
Joseph was thirty years old when he was presented before Pharaoh, king of Egypt. Joseph went out from Pharaoh’s presence and traveled throughout all Egypt.
During the seven years of abundance, the land produced crops.
He gathered all the food of the seven years in which there was abundance in the land of Egypt and stored food in the cities. In each city he stored the food from the fields surrounding it.
Joseph gathered grain like the sand of the sea, in very great quantities, until it could no longer be counted, for it was beyond numbering.
Joseph had two sons before the seven years of famine came. Asenath, the daughter of Potiphera, priest of Heliopolis, bore them to him.
Joseph named his firstborn Manasseh, for he said, “God has made me forget all my troubles and all my father’s troubles.”
He named the second Ephraim, for he said, “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.”
The seven years of abundance that had been in the land of Egypt came to an end.
The seven years of famine began to come, just as Joseph had said. There was famine throughout the whole land, for no bread could be found anywhere in the land of Egypt.
The whole land of Egypt suffered hunger, and all the people cried out to Pharaoh for bread. Pharaoh said to all the Egyptians, “Go to Joseph and do whatever he tells you.”
There was famine over the face of the whole earth. Joseph opened all the grain storehouses and sold grain to all the Egyptians. The famine grew severe throughout the whole land of Egypt.
All the countries came to Egypt to buy from Joseph, because the famine was growing severe throughout the whole earth.
Jacob saw that there was grain for sale in the land of Egypt. Jacob said to his sons, “Why are you idle?”
Look, I hear that there is grain in Egypt. Go down there and buy us a little food, so that we may live and not die.
Joseph’s ten brothers went down to buy grain from Egypt.
But Jacob did not send Benjamin, Joseph’s brother, with the brothers, for he said, “Perhaps some illness might befall him.”
The sons of Israel came to buy grain among the other travelers, for there was famine in the land of the Canaanites.
Joseph was the ruler of the land, and he sold grain to all the people of the land. Joseph’s brothers came and bowed down with their faces low to the ground.

When Joseph saw his brothers, he recognized them, but treated them as strangers and spoke very harshly to them. He said, “Where do you come from?” They said, “From the land of the Canaanites, to buy food.”
Joseph recognized his brothers, but they did not recognize him.
Joseph remembered the dreams he had seen and said to them, “You are spies, and you have come to inspect the ways into and out of this country.”
They said, “No, lord. Your servants have come to buy food.”
“We are all sons of one man. We are peaceful men, and your servants are not spies.”
He said to them, “No, you have come to inspect the ways into and out of this land.”
They said, “We, your servants, are twelve brothers, sons of one man in the land of the Canaanites. The youngest is with his father today, and the other is no longer among us.”
Joseph said to them, “That is just what I told you: you are spies.”
“And by this prove yourselves: as surely as Pharaoh lives, you will not leave here unless your youngest brother comes here.”

“Now send one of you to bring your brother, while you remain in custody until your words are shown to be true, to see whether you speak honestly. If not, then [?] I swear by Pharaoh’s life that you are spies.”
He put them in prison for three days.
On the third day Joseph said to them, “Do this and live, for I too fear God.”
“If you are peaceful men, let one of your brothers remain here in prison, while you take away the grain you have bought.”
“Bring your youngest brother to me, and your words will be found trustworthy. Otherwise, you will die.” They did so.

They said to one another, “Yes, we are guilty concerning our brother, for we disregarded the distress of his soul when he pleaded with us, and we did not listen to him. That is why this distress has come upon us.”
Reuben answered and said to them, “Did I not speak to you and say, ‘Do not sin against the boy’? But you did not listen to me. And now his blood is being demanded.”
They did not know that Joseph understood them, for there was an interpreter between them.
Joseph withdrew from them and wept. Then he returned to them and spoke with them. He took Simeon from among them and bound him before their eyes.
Joseph ordered that their containers be filled with grain, that each man’s money be put in his sack, and that they be given provisions for the journey. This was done for them.
Each loaded his donkey, and they departed from there.
When one of them opened his sack to give his beast food at the lodging place, he saw his bundle of money, for it was in the mouth of his sack.

He said to his brothers, “My money has been returned to me, and look, it is here in my sack!” Their minds were stunned, and they were troubled, saying to one another, “What is this that God has done to us?”
They came to their father Jacob in the land of Canaan and told him everything that had happened to them, saying:
The man who is lord of the land spoke harshly to us and put us in prison as spies of the land.
We said to him, “We are peaceful men, not spies.”
“We are twelve brothers, sons of our father. One is no longer with us, and the youngest is now with our father in the land of Canaan.”
The man who is lord of the land said to us, “By this I will know that you are peaceful men: leave one of your brothers here with me, and take the grain you have bought home to your households.
“Bring your youngest brother to me, and I will know that you are not spies but peaceful men. Then I will also give this brother back to you, and you may trade here in the land.”
When they emptied their sacks, each man's bundle of money was in his sack. When they and their father saw their bundles of money, they were very afraid.
Their father Jacob said to them, “You have deprived me of my children. Joseph is no longer with us, Simeon is no longer with us, and you will take Benjamin too. All this has come upon me.”
Reuben spoke to his father and said, “Kill my two sons if I do not bring him back to you. Entrust him to my care, and I will bring him back to you.”

He said, “My son will not go down with you, because his brother has died, and he alone is left. If he should fall ill on the journey you are taking, you will bring my old age down to the realm of the dead in sorrow.”
The famine grew more and more severe in the land.
When they had finished eating the grain they had brought from the land of Egypt, their father said to them, “Go again and buy a little food.”
Judah spoke to him and said, “The man solemnly warned us, saying, ‘You must not see my face unless your youngest brother is with you.’
“So if you send our brother with us, we will go down and buy food.”
“But if you do not send our brother with us, we will not go, because the man told us, ‘You must not see my face unless your youngest brother is with you.’”
Israel said, “Why have you brought trouble upon me by telling the man that you have a brother?”

They said, “The man questioned us closely about ourselves and our family, asking, ‘Is your father still alive? Do you have a brother?’ We told him in answer to his questions. How could we have known that he would tell us, ‘Bring your brother’?”
Judah said to his father Israel, “Send the boy with me, and let us get up and go, so that we may live and not die—we, you, and our possessions.
“I will guarantee his safety; you may hold me responsible for him. If I do not bring him back to you and set him before you, I will bear the blame forever.
“If we had not delayed, we would have returned here twice by now.”
